Expiring Relief

What Hawaiʻi’s working families lose when the 2023 expansions of the earned income tax credit and the food/excise tax credit expire after 2027, and what renewing them would cost.

Hawaiʻi Appleseed · Model run September 25, 2026 · Tax years 2028 to 2031

$78 million
Less for working families in tax year 2028, and what renewal would cost the state.
167,000
Households that lose part of a credit in 2028.
$948
Average loss for a single-parent household that loses.
6,500
More people in poverty, including about 2,100 children.

What Act 163 Did

IN 2023 THE LEGISLATURE DOUBLED Hawaiʻi’s two main tax credits for working families.1 Act 163 raised the state earned income tax credit from 20 percent to 40 percent of the federal credit, which already went only to people who work.2 It also more than doubled the refundable food/excise tax credit, which offsets the general excise tax low-income households pay on groceries and other necessities, and extended it $10,000 further up the income scale.3

Both expansions were temporary. Act 163 is repealed on December 31, 2027, and both credits return to their earlier form for tax year 2028. A 2026 bill to extend them was not enacted.4 The earned income tax credit stays refundable, but at 20 percent of the federal credit.

What Families Lose

WHEN THE EXPANSIONS EXPIRE, working families will receive about $78 million less in tax year 2028: $44 million from the earned income tax credit and $34 million from the food/excise tax credit. Renewing both would cost the state the same amount, about $307 million over tax years 2028 to 2031.5

The food/excise credit’s dollar amounts and income limits are not adjusted for inflation, so as wages rise, fewer households qualify and each credit buys less. Under the expanded table the credit would pay $53 million in 2028 and $47 million in 2031. The earned income tax credit follows the federal credit, which is indexed.

Who Loses

THE LOSS FALLS HARDEST ON FAMILIES WITH CHILDREN and the lowest incomes. In 2028, 72 percent of households in the lowest-income fifth lose part of a credit, an average of $549 each, and that fifth bears 50 percent of the total. Single-parent households that lose give up $948 on average, as Figure 2 shows.

Households are ranked by the combined income of everyone in them. Many Hawaiʻi households include several tax filers, so a grown child or grandparent with a low income can qualify on their own return in a household near the top of the ranking; that is why 25 percent of the top fifth lose some credit.

More Families in Poverty

LOSING THE EXPANSIONS PUSHES an estimated 6,500 more people below the poverty line in 2028, about 2,100 of them children, and deepens poverty for families already below it by $21 million. The state poverty rate rises from 10.7 percent to 11.2 percent. For single parents and their children it rises from 22.1 percent to 24.3 percent.

These figures use the Census Bureau’s Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts tax credits and public benefits as income and adjusts for Hawaiʻi’s cost of living. Because the counts come from a survey sample, they are rounded to the nearest hundred. The estimate is static: it does not count parents who leave work when the credit shrinks, which the model’s separate analysis of the earned income tax credit finds would add to the total.

How These Estimates Are Made

THE MODEL BUILDS Hawaiʻi tax households from the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey microdata, with each dependent’s age and relationship, projects their incomes forward with Congressional Budget Office growth rates, and computes the federal earned income tax credit, matched to IRS counts of Hawaiʻi claimants. Each state credit is then computed under both laws from the statute’s own schedules.

Not every eligible household claims a credit. The model sets each credit’s claim rate so that 2023, the first year of the expansions, matches what the Department of Taxation actually paid, then holds that rate fixed.6 As a test, the same rate applied to 2022, before the expansion, reproduces that year’s food/excise credit under the old table within 2 percent (Table 5).
